Clarke explains the placing by a custom rather than a theology: all nations dedicated the spoils of war to their gods, partly as a gratitude offering for help supposed to have been given and partly as proof that the conquerors' gods were the stronger, and he traces it from Saul's armour hung in the temple of Ashtaroth and Goliath's sword laid up in the tabernacle down to the depositing of captured colours and standards in his own day. The intention here, he has no doubt, was to insult the God of Israel and terrify his people. Henry allows two readings and prefers the second. They may have set the ark beside Dagon as a sacred thing to be honoured with him, since the gods of the heathen were never thought averse to partners and the nations would multiply their gods rather than change them — but that mistakes the God of Israel, who is not worshipped at all if he is not worshipped alone. More likely it was a trophy, set there as they had boasted over Samson. Keil states the outcome in advance: the Philistines were to get no pleasure from their booty, but to learn that the God who gave up his greatest sanctuary to humble his own degenerate nation was the only true God.

Ellicott fills a gap the writer leaves, since nothing is said of what became of Shiloh; from a psalm and two passages in Jeremiah he reconstructs a march on the sanctuary city, a massacre and the razing of the sacred buildings, and notes that its fate passed into a proverb — this house shall be like Shiloh — while insisting the national life was not extinguished. Then the mornings. Gill supposes the men of Ashdod came early either to pay their devotions before business or to offer the morning sacrifice, and on the second day adds that they may have come out of curiosity, to see whether the ark and Dagon agreed better together. Everyone notes that the first fall was taken for an accident and the idol set up again; Keil says they were obliged to give up that notion on the second morning, when the god lay broken. Wesley reads the mutilation as a statement rather than damage: the head is the seat of wisdom and the hands the instruments of action, and both were cut off to show that he had neither wisdom nor strength to defend himself or his worshippers — so that the priests, by concealing his shame the first time, only made it more evident and infamous.

What was left is a matter of Hebrew. Keil observes that the word in the last clause is used appellatively, meaning the fishy part, from the noun for a fish, and dismisses an inference of Thenius that the small dimensions of ancient temple recesses would explain how the severed pieces came to fall on the threshold. Clarke says the same and reaches for Horace's line about a shape that ends in a fish though the upper part is a beautiful woman, concluding that everything human in the idol was broken off from what resembled a fish, and that here was proof the affair was not accidental. Then the custom, which Clarke and Ellicott both follow forward. Because the god's hands broke on the threshold, the threshold became sacred and neither priests nor worshippers would tread on it — so that by an observance of their own they perpetuated their own disgrace and the superiority of the God of Israel. Both find the practice still alive centuries later in Zephaniah's threat against those who leap over the threshold, Ellicott dating it to the reign of Josiah. Clarke carries it further than Ellicott will go, noting that temple thresholds elsewhere were held sacred enough to be kissed, and that when Christianity became corrupted the same adoration of church thresholds appeared.

Henry sets the plague against what came before it: the fall of Dagon might have prevented all this had the people made a good use of it and repented, but where God's hand is lifted up and men will not see, they shall feel the weight of it. He distinguishes two visitations in the chapter rather than one, since some were destroyed outright and others smitten with the disease, and points to the verse which says expressly that those smitten with emerods were the men who did not die of the other stroke, which he takes to have been the pestilence. The Philistines had boasted of the slaughter their sword made among Israel; God lets them know that although he did not see fit to draw Israel's sword against them, since they were unworthy of the employment, he had a sword of his own. On what the disease was, Clarke reasons from the root, which means to be elevated, and settles on enlarged haemorrhoidal veins with frequent discharges of blood, accompanied by dysentery; Ellicott says the English word should simply be spelt as the medical one; and Wesley, following the phrase about the hidden parts, notes that this is the worst kind, both because the pain is sharper and because the malady lies further out of the reach of remedies.

The Greek and Latin versions carry an addition here that the Hebrew does not, saying that mice were produced in the land and there was the confusion of a great death in the city, and the two commentators who report it draw opposite conclusions from the same evidence. Clarke, following Houbigant, contends that the words stood originally in the Hebrew text and were lost, and that they supply what is otherwise unexplained — why golden mice were sent back with the ark in the next chapter along with the images of the tumours. Ellicott reverses the causation entirely: the translators, failing to understand why golden mice should be offered, added the sentence by way of explanation, apparently on the strength of a received tradition. He supports his own reading of the offering from elsewhere, noting that the mouse was an old symbol of pestilence on the testimony of Herodotus and of the hieroglyphics. Clarke has a further textual note in the same vein at Gath, where the Vulgate adds, without warrant in the Hebrew, that the sufferers made themselves seats of skins — for sitting more easily, he explains, on account of the malady.

Keil is the only voice to reconstruct what the Philistine lords were thinking when they moved the ark on. They probably supposed that the calamity did not really proceed from the ark at all; or that if it did, the trouble was that Ashdod in particular was hateful to the God of Israel; or that the Dagon of Ashdod was simply the weaker god. Sending it to Gath was therefore a test of all three suppositions at once. Clarke marks the moment the test resolved, when the men of Ashdod confessed that the hand was sore upon them and upon Dagon their god: the end was completely answered, since they now saw that they had not prevailed against Israel because their god was the stronger. Gill supplies the geography, that Ekron lay about ten miles from Gath and was the city where Baalzebub, the god of the fly, was worshipped — which sits oddly beside a plague of mice and a nation begging to be rid of it. Keil renders the Ekronite panic closely: they cried out before the ark was well arrived, speaking as one man, that it had been brought to slay them and their people, and what filled the city was a confusion of death, an alarm produced by many sudden deaths together.
